source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.8, printed pages 14-15: metallic character and its trends (Figure 1.3, carried by the trends original). The print's garbled sentence on 'm.c decrees' is given in plain words.

blocks.text: The metallic character of an element is its tendency to lose electrons. Elements on the left side of the periodic table have a greater tendency to lose their outermost electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration, while elements on the right tend to gain electrons. So elements on the left are metals that form positive ions, and elements on the right, particularly in the right corner, are non-metals that form negative ions; the metallic character of an element depends largely on its valence shell electronic configuration.

blocks.alt: A periodic table shaded from pink at the lower left (most metallic) to pale blue at the upper right (most non-metallic). Red arrows show metallic character increasing to the left across a period and down a group; a blue arrow shows non-metallic character increasing to the right and up a group.
blocks.caption: General trends for the metallic character of elements (original diagram after Figure 1.3).

blocks.text: Across a period from left to right the nuclear charge increases and the atomic size decreases, which pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus and makes it harder for the atom to lose electrons, so the metallic character decreases. Down a group the metallic character increases, because the atomic size and the shielding effect increase and reduce the nuclear attraction on the valence electrons. The increase in metallic character, the ease of losing an electron, makes the element more reactive: cesium is far more reactive and electropositive than sodium or lithium.
